## $2\times2$ determinants

The determinant of a $2\times2$ matrix 
$$
A = \begin{bmatrix} a&b\\c&d \end{bmatrix}
$$
can be computed by $ad-bc$ and characterized as the area of the parallelogram spanned by the columns of $A$. The objective of this set of class notes is to gain some intuition around this via the geometric effect of the elementary matrices.

## Elementary matrices

The elementary matrices are exactly those matrices obtained 
An elementary matrix can be obtained by applying an elementary row operation to the identity matrix. For example,

$$
\begin{bmatrix} 1&0\\0&1 \end{bmatrix}
\xrightarrow{\,-2R_1+R_2 \to R_2\,}
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\-2&1\end{bmatrix}
$$

In addition, multiplication by an elementary matrix performs that operation! For example, 
$$
\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\-2&1\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\-2a+c&-2b+d\end{bmatrix}.
$$

As a result, the nonsingular matrices are exactly those matrices that can be expressed as a product of elementary matrices. Furthermore, it's not hard to show that 
$$
\det(E_1E_2) = \det(E_1)\det(E_2)
$$
for elementary matrices $E_1$ and $E_2$. Thus, this result extends to all nonsingular matrices.

## Geometric illustrations

### Stretch

The unit square is shown below. Multiplying by the elementary matrix
$$\begin{bmatrix}2&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$$
increases the area of the matrix by the factor 2, as well as the value of the determinant.

```{ojs}
viewof updateStretch = Inputs.toggle({label: "Apply:"})
```

```{ojs}
picStretch = make_one_step_transition_pic([[2,0],[0,1]])
```


### Reflect

If the sign of one of the diagonal entries is negative, we change the orientation of the image and the sign of the determinant
$$\begin{bmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$$


```{ojs}
viewof updateReflect = Inputs.toggle({label: "Apply:"})
```

```{ojs}
picReflect = make_one_step_transition_pic([[-1,0],[0,1]])
```

### Reflect diagonally

Swapping two rows in the identity matrix also induces a change and orientation and sign
$$
\begin{bmatrix} 1&0\\0&1 \end{bmatrix}
\xrightarrow{\,R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2\,}
\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix}
$$


```{ojs}
viewof updateReflect2 = Inputs.toggle({label: "Apply:"})
```

```{ojs}
picReflect2 = make_one_step_transition_pic([[0,1],[1,0]])
```

### Skew 

A skew preserves area.
$$
\begin{bmatrix} 1&0\\0&1 \end{bmatrix}
\xrightarrow{\,-2R_2+R_1\to R_1\,}
\begin{bmatrix}1&-2\\0&1\end{bmatrix}
$$


```{ojs}
viewof updateSkew = Inputs.toggle({label: "Apply:"})
```

```{ojs}
picSkew = make_one_step_transition_pic([[1,-2],[0,1]])
```

To understand the result, recall that *every time* we apply matrix multiplication to our image of the unit circle, the legs of the image are exactly the columns of the matrix.


### Project 

Projection flattens area and resulrs in a determinant of zero.
$$\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$$


```{ojs}
viewof updateProject = Inputs.toggle({label: "Apply:"})
```

```{ojs}
picProject = make_one_step_transition_pic([[1,0],[0,0]])
```
